gap: No result ChatGPT got states which 14-inch MacBook Pro chips can run both screens of a two-screen extender with the lid open: Apple's specs give the base M3 14-inch one external display with the lid open (the second only with the lid closed), while the base M4 and M5 14-inch drive two.
standout_why: Rival pages compared: theofficejournal.com (14-inch and USB-C extender pages) and itechguides.com 15 Best (all cited or ranked first). The Office Journal says only that a USB-C port needs DisplayPort Alt Mode to carry video, and its USB-C page never mentions DisplayLink, MST, Mac display limits or mirroring. iTechGuides says to 'check the laptop manufacturer's documentation for supported internal-plus-external and external-only display counts' but gives no counts for any Mac. ChatGPT's answer only says 'M1–M3 … check external-display limits'. Our own page, dealectric.com/best-laptop-screen-extender (result 3), covers MST, quoting ViewSonic and Xebec, and the M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air limits. It does not give the 14-inch MacBook Pro chip-by-chip limits, which are the Macs this question is about. One result, Macworld's Trio 3 Pro review (not in ChatGPT's results), even suggests a base M3 drives both Trio screens, which Apple's M3 14-inch spec contradicts.
decides: For a 14-inch MacBook Pro with the base M3 chip, any two-screen extender driven natively (Trio 3 Pro without its driver, FOPO S7 or S1 if they need one video connection per screen, Aura Dual Boost) lights only one added screen with the lid open. The one-screen Mobile Pixels Duex Max DS is the pick that works on every 14-inch MacBook Pro. A dual pick needs a base M4 or M5 (or a Pro/Max chip), or a display driver. On Windows 14-inch laptops the test is one video-capable USB-C port (or HDMI) per added screen. macOS does not split one MST port into separate desktops (Plugable), so a dual extender run from one cable without a driver shows the same image on both screens on a Mac.

findings.label: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M3, Nov 2023): external displays
findings.value: One external display up to 6K at 60 Hz; second external display only with the lid closed (up to 5K at 60 Hz)
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M3, Nov 2023) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's words: 'One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz'; 'Close the MacBook Pro lid to use a second external display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz'. Ports: two Thunderbolt / USB 4 ports with DisplayPort, plus one HDMI. With the lid open, a two-screen extender gets only one screen natively.

findings.label: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M4, 2024): external displays
findings.value: Up to two external displays up to 6K at 60 Hz over Thunderbolt; three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports with native DisplayPort 1.4 output
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M4, 2024) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's words: 'Up to two external displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt'; 'Support for native DisplayPort 1.4 output over USB-C'. The page states no lid-closed condition, so both added screens of a native two-screen extender can run with the laptop's own screen on.

findings.label: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M5): external displays
findings.value: Up to two external displays over any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI, with the built-in display at full native resolution; three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M5) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's words: 'Supports up to two external displays over any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI ports'; 'Simultaneously supports the built-in display at full native resolution'; also 'Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port' (Apple does not say how; this page does not mention MST).

findings.label: Display limit depends on model and on each display's resolution and refresh rate
findings.value: Apple says the number of displays depends on the Mac model and on each display's resolution and refresh rate
findings.source_title: How many displays can be connected to MacBook Pro - Apple Support
findings.note: Index page that links to the per-model specs above; it gives no counts itself.

findings.label: macOS and DisplayPort MST (one port, two screens)
findings.value: macOS does not support MST for separate extended displays; two monitors on one USB-C port mirror
findings.source_title: Plugable KB: If I connect the Plugable USBC-MSTH2 to a MacBook would I be able to see two distinct screens or would both screens display the same content
findings.note: Plugable's words: 'macOS does not support MST for multiple independent extended displays through standard MST adapters'; 'the external monitors will mirror the same content instead of displaying separate desktops.' Hardware maker's statement, not Apple's.

findings.label: Video path on a 14-inch MacBook Pro (Macworld, Simon Jary)
findings.value: Two included USB-C cables, one per screen; no driver needed if the laptop has two DisplayPort-enabled USB-C ports; otherwise free driver software 'rather like DisplayLink'
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review - Macworld (Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Jary tested it on a 14-inch MacBook Pro. He says plain (non-Pro/Max) M1 and M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo are limited to one monitor. He also says it is 'compatible with 13-inch to 16-inch MacBooks' (Macworld's range; Mobile Pixels' own range is in our record as 15–16 inch) and weighs 4.13 lb (1.9 kg). His suggestion that a standard M3 drives both screens without software conflicts with Apple's M3 14-inch spec (one external display with the lid open).
